EDIT: Contribution is open to new iterations of this account as well as the /v/shortstories community. Try to keep everything structured so it reads in order.

I am some iteration of CommunityAccount. The account is an experiment of sorts, so I'm starting an experiment within the experiment. I'm going to start a short story here and encourage future incarnations to contribute as well. One paragraph at a time. The only question is..

How should my story begin? Is it a mystery? A tale of frights? Does it involve unbelievable fantasy, magic or strange accounts of beings from other worlds? I can tell you with a straight face, my story has all of that and more.

It began when I was a small child, following my father around after a dig. He would bring home the strangest artifacts from all over the world and I would find a great deal of entertainment from pocketing some small, strange object and sneaking off to play with it.
An experiment in short story building. This may take a while.

As the saying goes, if I had known then what I know now... well you know the rest. Looking back, I have to admit there was nothing about that particular artifact to indicate that it was any different than all the rest of the baubles and trinkets had I swiped from my father's collections. It seemed a perfectly ordinary idol or statuette about 6 inches tall. It was roughly chipped from a piece of obsidian, which is what first caught my attention. I liked the way the light reflected off its angles and edges. It depicted an owl, or at least that was my impression. It wasn't until years later that I came to appreciate the skill and patience it must have taken to shape even that vague form by patiently chipping away at the volcanic glass. So, there was nothing about it that seemed out of place.

At least, not in the beginning.

I think it had might have started as early as the end of June, but I can't be certain. Perhaps some of the dreams I had back then were just that, dreams. Perhaps they weren't, but I do not have the courage to admit to myself that I might have known what was going on all along and yet did nothing. I prefer to think of my younger self as a fool rather than a coward, a fool dressing the owl statue in a tiny overcoat from a teddy bear but not as someone who would shy away from adventure. As it so happened, the adventure was right around the corner, and, as all good adventures do, it had started with a death.

the buildup was as innocuous, as the mailman. father began almost attacking certain dig sites, around the world and late into the night, as if some critical piece of the puzzle was gone. he looked exhausted every time he sat down to eat dinner, and eventually he just ate out at his research tent each night. we were in morocco then, the chest pains started prompting small complaints from him, and only six months later, he was gone from the world with an end mysterious enough be seen only as a heart attacks close cousin. the next domino fall, was attending the funeral.

I was only 8 years old at the time of my father's funeral, but when I walked up to his casket and looked down I did not recognize the man inside. It had been so long since I last saw him and his features had changed so much that he looked like a completely different person, I was 6 when I saw him last. It was normal for me to not see my father for months at a time because of his archeological work, but when he came back from those long trips away he would always bring back a souvenir for his collection that he found on the site like the obsidian owl, which was the only thing I had to remember him by. In the 2 years I hadn't seen my father it looked as if he had aged 10, his wrinkles were more profound his hair was completely grey and his beard had grown out to a wild and scraggly state. I remember his dead face even to this day, but I also remember the countless times he made my mother cry by leaving home so frequently and I hated him for it, I hated him for not being there when we needed him, but most of all I hated him for not saying goodbye before he left. That night after the funeral when we got home I immediately went to my room walked over to the nightstand and grabbed the owl statuette, I stared at it for a long while then I placed it inside a shoebox and hid it in my closet. That night I heard my mother cry herself to sleep for what seemed like forever so I decided to go in her room, climb up into her bed and cry with her. I didn't get any sleep that night and the next time I would see the owl again would be on my 18th birthday...when the dreams came back only to become more vivid and nightmarish then I had remembered.

Music. Cake. Dancing. Eighteen birthdays were enough for me to play along to the rhythm well. Drinking. Walking. Laughing. Falling. Eyes closed. Alarm rings. Morning.

The door shook with a steady knock and jarred open, allowing a piercing ray to enter through the slit and land where I lay my head. My mother poked her head through the door, proclaimed a muffled greeting through the hands which I had clasped over my face, before leaving for work. The door's close allowed me to fall back into the dark comfort of the room, my eyes twitched before becoming heavy, with a headache still present from the previous night I closed my eyes again and let sleep wash over me.

My mind slowed as I lay there, yet the ticking of the clock was different each time it sounded, every second was shorter than the last. The darkness of my inner eyelids seemed to warp and distort, as if I was running to them at a great speed. My heart rate increased as I noticed a shadow in the darkness, cold it stood and looked at me with a harsh glare, probing me with its gaze, twitching its feathers as it looked on.

It was only as it faded that I realised I was crying.
